excerpt: What makes Folly Road one of Charleston's most crash-prone corridors, and your options after a collision on James Island.
keyTakeaways: Folly Road is James Island's primary corridor and one of Charleston's most crash-prone roads — SCDOT counted 2,103 vehicle crashes on five miles of it from 2018 to 2022 — because of heavy traffic, uncontrolled left turns across its center turn lane, and dense commercial driveways. Common accidents include rear-end collisions, T-bone crashes at intersections, and pedestrian strikes. Liable parties may include other drivers, the City of Charleston, or SCDOT for road design deficiencies; claims against the City or SCDOT fall under the Tort Claims Act, which allows two years to sue. South Carolina's 3-year statute of limitations applies (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), and comparative fault bars recovery at 51% or more.

faqs.question: Why is Folly Road so dangerous for drivers?
faqs.answer: Folly Road is the only road on and off Folly Beach and James Island's main commercial spine, so beach traffic and local traffic share one five-lane corridor. It combines high-volume commuter traffic with tourist beach traffic, dense commercial driveways, a 45 mph limit that drops sharply at Folly Beach, limited shoulders for cyclists and pedestrians, and flooding in heavy rain. SCDOT counted 2,103 vehicle crashes on five miles of it between 2018 and 2022, and its safety audit singled out left-turn angle crashes as the ones that end in injuries and fatalities.

faqs.question: What should I do after a car accident on Folly Road?
faqs.answer: Move to safety if possible since secondary crashes are a real risk on this busy road. Call 911 for police and medical assistance. Seek medical attention within 24 hours even if symptoms seem minor. Photograph vehicle damage, road conditions, and injuries. Exchange information with the other driver. Identify witnesses. Do not give recorded statements to the other driver's insurance company. Contact a car accident lawyer promptly to preserve traffic camera and surveillance footage.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident claim after a Folly Road crash?
faqs.answer: South Carolina allows three years from the date of the accident for personal injury claims (S.C. Code section 15-3-530) and three years from the date of death for wrongful death claims. A claim against SCDOT, the City of Charleston or Charleston County must be filed within two years (S.C. Code section 15-78-110). However, critical evidence like traffic camera footage and business surveillance video is often overwritten within days, so contacting a lawyer within the first few days is essential.

faqs.question: Can I recover damages if I was partially at fault for the accident?
faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.) that allows recovery as long as your fault is less than 51 percent. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. Insurance companies frequently argue that drivers on Folly Road were following too closely or were distracted, but an attorney can counter these arguments with evidence.

faqs.question: Can I sue a bar on Folly Beach if a drunk driver caused my accident?
faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but a bar or restaurant that knowingly serves a visibly intoxicated patron violates S.C. Code sections 61-4-580 and 61-6-2220, and the courts treat that as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club; Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill). For crashes after January 1, 2026, section 61-2-147 can make the establishment jointly liable for half of your actual damages when a verdict is returned against both it and the DUI driver. Folly Road is the only road home from Folly Beach's bars, which makes over-service a live question in DUI crashes on this corridor.

faqs.question: What types of injuries are common in Folly Road car accidents?
faqs.answer: Common injuries include traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, broken bones, internal organ damage, whiplash and soft tissue injuries, and in the most severe cases, wrongful death. T-bone (angle) collisions at intersections tend to produce the most severe injuries. Pedestrian and bicycle crashes on Folly Road are also disproportionately severe: SCDOT's road safety audit counted 15 pedestrian and 21 bicycle crashes on the corridor between 2018 and 2022, and three of its six fatal crashes killed pedestrians.
